title: The Power of Prompts to Reinforce New Behaviors
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note explains habit formation through the lens of prompts -- the triggers, like a red light or an alarm, that activate behavior automatically. It argues new habits fail most often because they lack a reliable prompt, and offers leaders two paths forward: attach a desired new behavior to an existing, reliable trigger, or deliberately design a brand-new prompt to cue the behavior. The piece walks through a concrete example -- building a habit of 'agreeing to disagree' during heated debates -- showing how specific existing moments, like a colleague repeating an argument, can serve as the trigger.
points: Prompts, or triggers, are described as the essential mechanism that activates most human behavior automatically.
New habits most often fail simply because they lack a reliable, attached prompt.
Two strategies are offered: piggyback a new habit onto an existing trigger, or design a brand-new one.
A worked example shows building an 'agreeing to disagree' habit tied to a colleague repeating an argument.
The piece frames small, deliberately designed prompts as powerful tools for building durable new habits.
quotes: Prompts activate behaviors. Without them, most behaviors and actions would never happen.
Without a reliable prompt, many actions don’t happen or are forgotten. This is especially true when we try to create a new habit.
Existing prompts might be: Any time a colleague repeats their argument or presents the same opinion three times in a row
Another option is to design a brand-new prompt that doesn’t naturally exist.
Small nudges can be powerful aids for creating new patterns of behavior.
